items.title: VAST Ghana calls for comprehensive excise tax reforms in 2027-2030 Budget Statement
items.description: The Vision for Accelerated Sustainable Development Ghana (VAST Ghana) has called on the Ministry of Finance to introduce comprehensive excise tax reforms in the 2027-2030 Budget to reduce the growing burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs). A statement copied to the Ghana News Agency by Ms Jennifer Maame Ama Owusu, Communications Manager, VAST Ghana, said the excise tax reform would help protect vulnerable populations and mobilise sustainable domestic resources for healthcare financing. The statement recommended that the Ministry of Finance adopt a comprehensive health tax reform as a strategic fiscal and public health priority. The VAST Ghana called for an extension of the hybrid excise tax structure to all alcoholic beverages (Beer, wine, cider, and ready-to-drink alcoholic products) rather than limiting the reform to spirits. Others were the incorporation of alcohol-by-volume (ABV) principles so that products are taxed according to their alcohol content, and the adoption of a minimum pricing policy to complement excise taxation. It further recommended the increase of the specific tobacco excise tax from GHc 0.28 to GHc 1.00 per cigarette stick to ensure total taxes reach 75 per cent of the retail price, and upward review of the ad valorem tax from 50 per cent to 100 per cent. It said this reform would substantially increase the price of cigarettes, reduce affordability, and strengthen the health impact of tobacco taxation. The statement also called for the abolition of the excise taxation on e-cigarettes and e-liquids, adding that, “Ghana’s public health and fiscal frameworks should not create a situation in which products that are prohibited under the Public Health Act 2012 (Act 851) are simultaneously presented within the excise tax system as taxable commodities.” It stated that removing these products from the excise tax schedule would improve policy coherence and strengthen enforcement. It urged for the reintroduction of the 20 per cent tax on fruit juices in the interest of public health, while the Ministry introduces a hybrid excise tax for all Sugar-Sweetened Beverages (SSB) products. The statement called for earmarking a defined proportion of revenue generated from tobacco, alcohol, SSB, and other health taxes to support NCD prevention, health promotion, tobacco and alcohol control programmes, and other priority health interventions like the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, Free Primary Healthcare policy, among others. It noted that the 2027 to 2030 Budget framework provides Ghana with an opportunity to institutionalise health taxation as a core component of fiscal policy, NCD prevention, and sustainable health financing. “The evidence is increasingly clear that well-designed health taxes reduce consumption of harmful products while generating public revenue,” it stated, adding that WHO’s ‘3 by 35’ Initiative places the taxation approach at the centre of global efforts to reduce NCDs and strengthen domestic financing. VAST Ghana therefore called on the Ministry of Finance to make these reforms a central component of Ghana’s domestic resource mobilisation and public health strategy.

items.title: ‘No-fees-stress’ policy boosts tertiary education enrollment – SDA College Vice Principal
items.description: The No-Fees-Stress Policy has boosted access to tertiary education, with beneficiaries at the SDA College of Education expressing appreciation to the government for easing the financial burden on students. Dr Gifty Seiwaa Nyarko, the Vice Principal of the SDA College of Education, Asokore – Koforidua in the Eastern region, said the college recorded 470 beneficiaries under the policy during the 2025/2026 academic year, all of whom were first-year students. Dr Nyarko, who was speaking in an interview with the Ghana News Agency (GNA), added that the beneficiaries comprised 160 males and 310 females. She described the high patronage as a demonstration of students’ understanding of the importance of taking advantage of available government interventions to pursue higher education. She advised beneficiaries to use the money provided by the government judiciously, since their academic user fees had already been covered under the policy. “The government had already supported you financially, so do not misuse the money given to you by your parents. Use it for things that can support your stay on campus and enhance your studies,” she said. The Vice Principal expressed gratitude to the government for the financial relief provided to students. Ms Esther Ansah, a first-year Bachelor of Education student in Early Grade Education, notes that the policy has made it possible for her to pursue her dream career in tertiary education, without any financial difficulty of paying academic user fees. “If the policy had not been introduced, I would not have been able to afford the fees at this initial stage. This would have disrupted my career,” she said. Mr Samuel Okai Ntiri, a beneficiary pursuing Primary Education, also noted that although some money had been provided by his family for his upkeep, it would not have been enough if he were to pay academic user fees. President John Dramani Mahama launched the No-Fees-Stress Policy on July 4, 2025, at the SDA College of Education as part of efforts to increase enrolment in the country’s public tertiary institutions. The policy covers academic user fees for all first-year (Level 100) students in public tertiary institutions, while continuing students at Levels 200, 300 and 400 may access the Student Loan Plus or the regular Student Loan Trust Fund (SLTF) loan scheme for financial support.

items.title: La tragedia en Urda empuja a la ultraderecha a una espiral de brutalidad
items.description: “Óscar Puente, asesino”, “Partido Socialista, banda criminal” y —el ya clásico— “Pedro Sánchez, hijo de puta”, corea la multitud. Otras proclamas evidencian la presencia allí de ultranacionalistas de sangre y suelo : “Esta es nuestra tierra y hay que defenderla”. Son pasadas las 20 horas del miércoles, día del accidente de Urda (Toledo), y se han concentrado más de mil personas junto al Ministerio de Transportes en Madrid. Están convocadas por Falange, partido heredero de la histórica tradición política española hermana del fascismo, y Revuelta, una asociación vinculada en sus orígenes a Vox que usa argumentos raciales para sus mensajes xenófobos . Hay mucho rostro tapado y mucha ropa negra. Ante el lanzamiento de bengalas y el agolpamiento de manifestantes en el cordón policial, los agentes cargan. Indignado, Pedro Chaparro, presidente de Democracia Nacional , vocea: “Lo que ha ocurrido hoy es una matanza. Esto es de rebelión nacional. Señores, hay que alzarse”. Pablo González, líder de Revuelta, se graba un vídeo imputando al Gobierno las víctimas de Urda, pero también de la dana de Valencia y del accidente de tren de enero en Adamuz . El mensaje anunciado como un “homenaje” a las víctimas de Urda acaba mencionando la crisis de Ceuta y hasta el volcán de La Palma , en un totum revolutum de asuntos de los que culpa al Ejecutivo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La mayoría de la Diputación Permanente del Congreso exige la dimisión de Puente por el accidente de Urda
items.description: El ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, constatará este martes de nuevo en el Congreso que no cuenta con el respaldo de la mayoría del Parlamento. Será un mensaje claro. PP, Vox, PNV y Junts suman 35 de los 69 puestos de la Diputación Permanente del Congreso que representa en estos momentos preelectorales a las Cortes Generales y todos esos partidos exigirán su dimisión. Es posible, también, que se enfrente incluso a duras críticas y rechazo de socios de legislatura, como le ha pasado ya en otros momentos de este mandato, en el que ha sido reprobado siete veces por el Congreso y el Senado. El ministro ha comunicado públicamente que dispone del apoyo del presidente del Gobierno para continuar en su puesto y que entiende que debe seguir tras el accidente de Urda para ofrecer soluciones y alternativas a un siniestro que ha puesto en cuestión todo el sistema ferroviario español. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Una reconciliación antes del final
items.description: Sandra del Olmo llegó nerviosa a la cita en una cafetería. Le esperaba su padre, al que no había visto hacía un año. Desde que él hizo las maletas y se fue de casa, las cosas entre ellos ya nunca fueron iguales. Algo parecía roto. En el divorcio, ella tomó partido por su madre y eso la había distanciado irremediablemente de él. Ese día, delante de un café, no hablaron de nada importante, solo de asuntos cotidianos de sus vidas. A partir de ese momento se llamaron y se mensajearon más a menudo, y eso les trajo mucha paz a ambos. Volvieron a verse tres veces más. La última, la noche del 27 de octubre, cuando él aparcó en la puerta de su casa con las luces encendidas, sacó una maleta y se la dejó a ella hasta que regresase. Al día siguiente tenía que coger el AVE. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La investigación del siniestro de Urda analiza si Adif usó el protocolo erróneo más veces
items.description: La orden emitida desde el centro de control de la circulación ferroviaria de Adif en Madrid-Atocha, el pasado miércoles a las 8.36 horas , para que un AVE de Renfe que viajaba desde Madrid con destino Sevilla saliera con marcha normal (con límite en 200 kilómetros por hora) de una situación de parada tras la caída del sistema de señalización LZB va a ser diseccionada por la investigación del siniestro de Urda (Toledo). Fuentes cercanas a las pesquisas explican que también serán revisados, tanto por la autoridad independiente de investigación técnica AITAT como por la policía judicial, decenas de antecedentes similares en la misma línea Madrid-Sevilla con fallos en la tecnología LZB. Ese tren al que se permitió avanzar a toda velocidad colisionó con un Iryo detenido, causando 69 víctimas mortales. El gestor de la infraestructura Adif ha comenzado a recopilar documentación para su inmediato traspaso a la investigación. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Isabel Coixet: “Woody Allen se está llevando una pasta de nuestros impuestos para hacer su película”
items.description: En su último año de universidad, Isabel Coixet (Sant Adrià de Besòs, 66 años) se fue a estudiar a la Sorbona sin apenas hablar francés y con una beca que solo le alcanzaba para pagar cama y transporte. “Para comer no llegaba, me tuve que buscar la vida. items.title: La crisis del Constitucional refleja la polarización extrema en Polonia a un año de las legislativas
items.description: La disputa en torno al Tribunal Constitucional en Polonia ha devuelto el foco a la extrema polarización del país . Los insólitos acontecimientos ilustran la lucha entre dos bloques políticos irreconciliables. Por un lado, un Gobierno de coalición liberal capitaneado por Donald Tusk que decide hacerse por sorpresa y con mano dura con el control del alto tribunal, politizado y deslegitimado. Por otro, una derecha ultraconservadora que se aferra a las cuotas de poder que capturó con maniobras contrarias al Estado de derecho y un jefe de Estado capaz de abrirse paso por la fuerza en la institución que vela por el orden constitucional. items.title: Raquel Catalá, la jueza de la vivienda que aprieta las tuercas a la Administración para que no desahucie sin dar una alternativa estable
items.description: Raquel Catalá trabaja como una hormiguita desde hace cuatro años en el juzgado número 29 de lo Contencioso Administrativo de Madrid. Desde que llegó, con una energía que no le pasa desapercibida a nadie, puso el contador prácticamente a cero en esa plaza judicial, en la que los asuntos se acumulan en torres de carpetas, y llevando a todo el personal del juzgado a su ritmo, tan frenético como la rapidez con la que piensa su cabeza. Su talón de Aquiles han sido casi siempre los desahucios. Desde hace más de tres años, en sus autos, suele rechazar la ejecución de esa desgarradora medida, que consiste en expulsar a la gente de sus casas, por entender que se deja a los inquilinos, “sea cual sea su naturaleza y siendo okupas la mayor parte de las veces”, en situación de calle. Según la interpretación que hace esta magistrada valenciana de las leyes, no se puede echar a ninguna familia vulnerable (sin recursos económicos o con menores al cargo) sin ofrecerle al mismo tiempo una alternativa habitacional estable". Esa es la idea que atraviesa sus decisiones judiciales a este respecto, para las que se lee la letra más pequeña y realiza una aproximación integral a la problemática, incluyendo factores sociales y de género para delimitar competencias y responsabilidades de todas las partes implicadas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ceuta, tres meses después: entre el fin de la esperanza y las redadas policiales
items.description: Todos los termómetros en Ceuta lo certifican: las temperaturas se han desplomado. Más allá de las evidentes, las que marca el mercurio decretando chaquetas y chubasqueros, el clima de tensión social ha bajado muchos grados tres meses después de la entrada masiva de migrantes . Cuando se cumple un trimestre de aquello la ciudad ya es otra, transita una nueva fase que comenzó con el desalojo de los asentamientos de las playas y continuó con la expulsión de migrantes a Marruecos , un flujo diario que ya ha sacado a casi 14.000 personas por la frontera. Otras 7.000 continúan en los centros de acogimiento, y el Ejecutivo de Juan Jesús Vivas calcula que 4.000 más quedan sin identificar. Seguir leyendo

Allí Almudí, que está lejos de ser un exaltado izquierdista, no se cortó delante de lo más granado de la conservadora esfera judicial: “Me sume en una honda preocupación el austericidio que injustamente afecta al presente y al futuro de la educación universitaria pública, materializado en un recorte del 35% de los gastos de la facultad [desde julio de 2024]”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Mary Austin, la exprometida de Freddie Mercury que lleva años guardando su legado: “Nuestro amor era mucho más poderoso de lo que llegué a imaginar”
items.description: El fondo de pantalla en la videollamada con Mary Austin (Londres, 75 años), quien fue la primera pareja de Freddie Mercury , no revela más que una pared blanca y una silla de oficina. Responde, sin embargo, desde Garden Lodge , la mítica casa al oeste de Londres que heredó del cantante y que, por muchos años, llegó a tener más pinta de museo: colecciones japonesas, un jardín que parecía un santuario y el piano de cola Yamaha en el que el vocalista de Queen compuso algunas de las canciones más emblemáticas del siglo XX. Austin tiene los ojos amables y es introvertida por naturaleza. Con el estreno de la película Bohemian Rhapsody en 2018, su cara se volvió más familiar, pero son pocas las entrevistas y apariciones públicas que ha realizado. Su vida la ha dedicado a recordar al “amor de su vida”, como sigue llamando a Mercury, de quien fue su principal heredera cuando el cantante murió de sida , en noviembre de 1991. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Vice President urges prison officers to respect inmate dignity and support rehabilitation
items.description: Vice President Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang has urged Ghana Prisons Service officers to uphold inmates’ dignity and provide them with opportunities for rehabilitation and successful reintegration into society. She said humane treatment of inmates is a fundamental responsibility of the Service, stressing the need for prison officers to discharge their duties with professionalism, discipline, and respect for human rights. Prof. Opoku-Agyemang assured that the government remained committed to working with the Service to improve staff welfare, strengthen institutional capacity, provide essential equipment, and promote professional development. She was speaking at the graduation parade of 609 officer cadets from Intakes 33, 34 and 35 at the Premier Centre for Prisons and Correctional Innovations at Fumso in the Adansi Asokwa District of the Ashanti Region. The graduating cohort comprised 392 males and 217 females, who were commissioned as Assistant Superintendents of Prisons. The Vice President said the government recognised the importance of improving conditions in the country’s prisons to support effective rehabilitation and ensure that inmates had the opportunity to become productive members of society. She announced the commissioning of the Damongo Camp Prison and reaffirmed the government’s commitment to completing the remand facility at Nsawam. Prof. Opoku-Agyemang called for sustained efforts to improve case management, address overcrowding and develop viable alternatives to custodial sentencing. She appealed to the public to desist from stigmatising former inmates and instead support their reintegration into society after serving their sentences. The Vice President said the government had also provided tractors, fertilisers and other agricultural inputs to support farming activities in the prisons. She explained that the initiative was intended to increase food production within the facilities while equipping inmates with practical agricultural and vocational skills to improve their livelihoods after release. She stressed that accountability and public safety must remain central to prison administration, urging the Service leadership to ensure rehabilitation initiatives are supported by comprehensive staff training. “Promotion is not merely a reward for past achievements, but a solemn commitment to upholding even higher standards of duty,” she said. The Vice President was accompanied by the Minister for the Interior, Alhaji Mohammed Muntaka Mubarak, Mrs Patience Baffoe-Bonnie, Director-General of the Ghana Prisons Service, and other senior officials of the Service.

items.title: Reko Diq project may face further delay
items.description: Production at the Reko Diq copper-gold project could be delayed by two years to 2030, pending improved security in Balochistan and de-escalation in the Middle East crisis, according to government sources and industry insiders. War in the neighbouring Iran alongside persistent security challenges in Balochistan have reportedly pushed investors to adjust the original 2028 timeline. Canadian mining titan Barrick Mining (formerly Gold) Corporation is expected to resume full-scale development by mid-2027 following an ongoing internal project review. While the company has yet to issue an official announcement, its local officials express optimism that the multibillion-dollar venture remains on track. Despite the operational slowdown, the project management has retained all 700 permanent and roughly 2,000 contractual workers at the site, though some third-party service contracts were allowed to expire. Barrick, as well as senior federal and Balochistan provincial government officials, did not immediately respond to requests for their comment. Iran situation alongside persistent security challenges in Balochistan has reportedly pushed investors to adjust the 2028 timeline Despite recent timeline concerns, the company sources maintain that daily operations on the ground remain active. “Research, administrative work, and community development projects are progressing normally,” said a company employee speaking on condition of anonymity. “Speculation about the project’s future is baseless and fuelled by ill-informed or irresponsible elements.” Another official echoed this confidence, pointing out that nearly $1 billion has already been invested in the venture. “The project is technically viable and holds immense promise for all stakeholders. External factors may delay it, but the stakes are too high for any shareholder — whether the miner or the government — to walk away now.” Adding momentum to upcoming industry talks, Barrick Mining Chairman John L. Thornton is expected to visit Pakistan later this month to attend the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 in Islamabad. However, industry experts remain divided over the financial fallout of potential delays. A private-sector source involved in another Balochistan mining venture warned of severe cost overruns, advocating for a consortium of local companies to acquire a minority stake. “Even if work resumes within a year, project costs could rise by $8bn to $10bn. Further security deterioration or delays exceeding two years could render it prohibitively expensive,” he cautioned. Conversely, an industry insider with business ties to the Reko Diq Mining Company (RDMC) dismissed the $10bn cost escalation estimate as “bordering on absurdity.” “Delays might raise costs by 10 per cent at most — roughly $450 million to $900m,” he estimated, adding that sentiment surrounding the project had improved sharply in recent weeks. “A month ago, I would have been uncertain. Today, I am confident that work on Reko Diq will resume sooner than expected.” He also expressed regret that the operator reportedly plans to process only 30pc to 35pc of the copper-gold output in Pakistan — potentially routing the remainder to its Australian facility — rather than maximising domestic value addition. In February this year, Barrick Mining initiated a formal review of Reko Diq, announcing a slowdown in development and extending its assessment period through early 2027. Speaking at the Mining Forum Americas last month, the Barrick CEO offered no revised construction timelines, noting: “We are revisiting it because we need some sort of security improvement before we would embark on a full construction schedule.” Canada’s Barrick Mining holds a 50pc stake in the project, with the remaining half split equally between the Balochistan provincial government and three Pakistani state-owned entities: Pakistan Petroleum, Oil and Gas Development Company, and Government Holdings Private. As one of Pakistan’s most ambitious infrastructure endeavours, Reko Diq’s estimated Phase 1 investment has escalated from $4bn to $5.6bn. Phase 2 is projected to require another $3.5bn, pushing total capital expenditure to roughly $9.1bn, up from earlier estimates of around $7bn. Designed as a conventional open-pit mining and processing operation, the site will yield high-grade copper-gold concentrate. Initial capacity is set at 45m tonnes of ore annually, which is expected to double to 90m tonnes upon Phase 2 completion. While the mine was originally slated for a 40-year operational lifecycle, an updated feasibility study revised that figure to 37 years to account for higher throughput. However, ongoing exploration and resource development could potentially extend the mine’s lifespan up to 80 years. Beyond its export and revenue potential, Reko Diq is expected to generate 7,500 jobs during peak construction and sustain around 4,000 permanent positions once operational. Based on long-term commodity price assumptions, projected free cash flow over 37 years is estimated at $74bn. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 2nd, 2026

items.title: IMF mission wraps up Ghana PCI review this week as economic targets take centre stage
items.description: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission to Ghana is expected to conclude its first Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI) review engagement this week, with economic targets and the country’s macroeconomic framework likely to dominate the final discussions. Sources say the closing engagements will review Ghana’s performance against quantitative targets for the year ending September, along with policies to sustain recent economic gains. The mission is expected to hold a final round of discussions with Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson and Bank of Ghana Governor Dr Johnson Asiama. The team, led by Dr Ruben Atoyan, may also meet members of Parliament, including the Finance Committee. The final discussions follow engagements with civil society organisations and visits to facilities, including the Tema Oil Refinery. The mission has also discussed the banking sector, energy, Ghana’s debt position and ongoing reforms at some state-owned banks. What the team has covered so far Ghana’s fiscal performance, revenue mobilisation and preparations for the 2027 Budget have featured prominently in the discussions, sources say. The team has examined economic performance during the first nine months of the year and the policies needed to sustain recent gains. Further engagements are expected to cover expenditure management for the rest of the year and spending plans for 2027. These discussions come as the government prepares to prioritise infrastructure investment in the upcoming budget. On monetary policy, the mission has discussed Ghana’s inflation-targeting framework and foreign exchange arrangements. Sources say the team has also assessed the Bank of Ghana’s financial position, international reserves and measures to safeguard its independence. The review forms part of Ghana’s engagement with the IMF under the PCI, a framework designed to support economic stability and sustain policy reforms without providing direct funding. PCI programme and what it means for Ghana The PCI allows countries to maintain close policy engagement with the IMF without borrowing under the instrument. It supports the design and implementation of economic reforms. It also helps demonstrate policy credibility to investors and development partners. Its objectives include strengthening macroeconomic stability, addressing economic imbalances and building resilience against shocks. Although the instrument provides no direct financing, participating countries must pursue policies that meet standards comparable to those under IMF lending arrangements. The IMF assesses performance through scheduled reviews, typically every six months. The PCI requires approval from the IMF Executive Board. This distinguishes it from a Staff-Monitored Programme, an informal arrangement between IMF staff and a member country. For Ghana, the review provides an opportunity to demonstrate progress on policy commitments and reinforce confidence in its economic programme.

items.title: Zambia: Widespread Repression in Post-Election Crackdown
items.description: Click to expand Image A police vehicle on the outskirts of Lusaka, Zambia, August 14, 2026. © 2026 Alfonso Nqunjana/AP Photo Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members, lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August. The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices.The authorities should immediately halt the crackdown, allow access to lawyers and medical care to detainees, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses. (Johannesburg) – The Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities have also yet to credibly explain or investigate the killing of an opposition leader in contested circumstances. “Zambia’s government should break this dangerous cycle of repression,” said Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces.” President Hakainde Hichilema was reelected in the August 13 election, which observers said was marred by irregularities such as a suspension of counting and limited fundamental freedoms. From August 24 to 28, the authorities suspended judicial services and prevented legal challenges to the presidential election results, closing and cordoning off court premises. Zambian police stated that the closures were an “intelligence-led and preventive measure,” without providing details. Human Rights Watch documented 14 cases in August that appear to have been enforced disappearances, in which the authorities refused to reveal the situation and whereabouts of a detained person. Several of these people were initially forcibly disappeared for days. Victims, family members, and lawyers said that the military held some of them. Human Rights Watch also documented 61 cases in which detainees or their lawyers and relatives allege that they were beaten or otherwise violently abused during their arrest, in detention, or both. Eighteen have been charged with treason, with two also facing sedition charges. In many cases, the people detained were never charged with a crime while in others, the charges against them appear to be politically motivated. The government has not disclosed how many people were arrested during the crackdown or the charges against them, prompting concerns that the number of people detained is higher than presently known. Human Rights Watch has also documented two cases in which the Zambia-based relatives of government critics living abroad say government authorities harassed and threatened them. The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices, Human Rights Watch said. On September 11, the government announced the cancellation of six government critics’ passports, including that of an academic, Sishuwa Sishuwa, for “security reasons.” On August 14, security forces raided the home of the Tonse Alliance opposition leader, Brian Mundubile, in a suburb of Lusaka, the capital. Opposition members present allege that security forces killed a former government minister, Mutotwe Kafwaya, during the raid. Inspector General of the Zambia Police Service Graphel Musamba said members of a “joint intelligence-led operation” were met with “gunfire and resistance from unknown individuals” that “prompted officers to return fire,” and that Kafwaya had been killed in the process. Kafwaya’s fate was not known until August 19, after his wife filed a habeas corpus petition to compel authorities to disclose his whereabouts, bring him before court, and show sufficient and lawful cause for his continued detention. Public officials made contradictory statements about the raid and who was responsible for it. On August 15, the Zambia Information and Communications Technology Authority (ZICTA) sent out a text message to all registered phones in Zambia stating: “Beware of false reports of shootings and abductions. Stay calm and peaceful.” The Ministry of Information and Media dismissed reports of the raid and shooting as “disinformation intended to alarm and mislead the public.” The police also issued a media statement denying that there had been a raid and that Mundubile was in police custody. Police Inspector General Musamba later admitted that there had been a “joint security-led intelligence operation” at Mundubile’s home. Mundubile, who was later arrested and charged with treason, stated in a High Court petition that Human Rights Watch has seen that he saw a member of the military fatally shoot Kafwaya. Given the conflicting statements by government officials about who was responsible for the raid on Mundubile’s home and the circumstances surrounding Kafwaya’s killing, Zambian authorities should institute an independent, impartial, and thorough investigation into the matter, Human Rights Watch said. Detainees have implicated Zambia’s military in arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Forty-three opposition members acting as election monitors were detained on August 14. Their lawyer said their whereabouts had been unknown for eight days and that the police had denied holding them. When a lawyer finally saw them, he told Human Rights Watch that “most of them were swollen and had terrible injuries, including broken bones. They said they had been brutalized by the military.” Their lawyers filed a habeas corpus application and, on September 10, a court in Lusaka ordered their immediate release. Under Zambian law and international human rights law, all detainees have the right to due process, including to be promptly informed of the charges against them, to have access to counsel if charged with a crime, to have their detention reviewed by a judge, and to be presumed innocent. They should also have access to adequate medical care and be able to communicate with their families. In a September 2 call, the United Nations special rapporteur on the rights to freedom of assembly and of association said that the authorities should “release all political detainees, respect fundamental freedoms, and restore democratic accountability.” The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said in response that the call was “inaccurate, undiplomatic and falling short of the standards of objectivity, moderation and discretion expected of UN mandate holders.” The ministry said that being a member of opposition party “does not place a person beyond the reach of the law, nor does it convert a criminal suspect into a political detainee… The government is committed to ensuring that these protections are respected in every case, and Zambia’s courts are open to test them.” Zambia will serve as a member of the UN Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 term. As a council member, Zambia is expected to “uphold the highest standards in the promotion and protection of human rights.” “The Zambian government’s needs to end its brazen human rights crackdown,” Budoo-Scholtz said. “Leaders in Southern Africa and Zambia’s development partners should encourage President Hichilema to restore the rule of law and ensure that civic and political spaces are protected.” Enforced Disappearances, Including by Military Personnel Human Rights Watch documented 14 cases of apparent enforced disappearances of opposition members and supporters, including some in which the authorities denied holding people who were later produced after habeas corpus applications. The authorities claimed to have arrested 11 men during the August 14 raid on Mundubile’s home. Lawyers and family members of seven of the men said that they were made to lie down and were beaten using fists, rifle butts, and sticks, kicked by men in military uniform, then blindfolded and driven away in military vehicles. Victims and witnesses identified members of Zambia’s military through their uniforms and military vehicles. During the same raid, security forces picked up several opposition members and supporters and forcibly disappeared them for days before family members or their lawyers found them. They included Bishop Trevor Mwamba, an opposition leader; Patrick Mwansa, a leading opposition campaigner; and security aides Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chewe, Brazil Soko, Francis Mulenga, and Richard Banda. According to their lawyers and court documents seen by Human Rights Watch, the men were taken to a “military command center” where they were “screened and processed” then detained in “various police stations around Lusaka.” Lawyers and family members said they went around police stations in Lusaka looking for the detainees, but authorities denied holding the men. However, some were found days later at the same stations where the police had denied holding them. Mwansa’s family said he had a broken finger and swollen face when they finally located him four days later in Lusaka’s Central Police Station. On September 6, Mwansa was moved to a maximum security prison in Kabwe, 150 kilometers from Lusaka, and has not yet received medical treatment, a family member said. The family of Bishop Mwamba, president of the opposition United National Independence Party, who was also picked up during the raid at Mundubile’s home, said they searched for him in police stations in and around Lusaka for four days before locating him at Matero Police Station. Earlier, including on the day he was located, officers at Matero Police Station had denied holding Mwamba. “He had spent days without food and without taking his prescription medication,” the relative said. “The police had first denied [holding him] but we insisted to see him, because we had received an anonymous tip informing us that he was at Matero. When they brought him out and we asked what he was arrested for, police said they had no charge for him ‘because he was brought in by the military who asked us to keep him in the cells for them.’” On August 30, when the family took food and pain killers to Benard Chewe at Kabwata Police Station, where he had been detained, officers there told them that he had been moved but claimed that they did not know where. When the family traced him two days later to Mwembeshi Correctional Facility on the outskirts of Lusaka, they were denied access. Men in unmarked vehicles who introduced themselves as “state intelligence officers” picked up Harry Findlay, a Lusaka businessman and opposition supporter, from his residence on August 4, a family member said. Neither his lawyer nor family had access to him, and the authorities did not inform them of his whereabouts. Findlay’s lawyers sent two letters to Zambian authorities, on August 7 and August 17, requesting his whereabouts and calling for his immediate release and access to doctors, lawyers, and family. On August 20, Findlay was taken to court under a judge’s order to inquire into the legality of his detention. On August 29, he was charged with treason and moved to Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison, where he remains without trial. All the men detained in the August 14 raid were eventually charged with treason and remain in detention without having appeared in court. Human Rights Watch believes that in these cases, Zambian authorities are using treason charges, which are nonbailable, and sedition, which carries a heavy penalty, to stifle dissent and political opposition. On August 27, police arrested Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, and subsequently also charged them with treason and seditious practices. The charge sheet, which Human Rights Watch has seen, alleges that Mundubile and Zulu went on Facebook live on August 14 stating that the opposition had won the election. The government alleges that this was meant to “raise discontent or disaffection among the people of Zambia.” On September 22, the Law Association of Zambia raised concerns about prolonged detentions without court appearances. Zambia’s Human Rights Commission on September 3 said it was following 84 election-related detainees whose cases it cast as part of a “disturbing pattern of prolonged detention, delayed notification of charges, restricted access to family and legal representation and failure to bring detainees before a competent court without undue delay.” Abuse and Ill-Treatment in Custody Human Rights Watch documented that 61 people had been mistreated in custody by reviewing court documents and interviewing family members. Lawyers for the 43 opposition members acting as election monitors who were detained on August 14 said that state security agents kicked and beat them and denied them food during the first 8 days of their 21-day detention. Lawyers representing 18 detainees accused of treason state in court documents that the detainees were abused and assaulted in custody and denied medical attention. The lawyers also said 10 of the 18—George Chisanga, Patrick Mwansa, Trevor Mwamba, Francis Mulenga, Brazil Soko, Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chewe, Richard Banda, Emmanuel Mulenga, and Darius Mwila—had been restricted from accessing their lawyers or family members. In a court petition filed on September 11, Ezra Topola, Dickson Tembo, and Victor Muzyamba alleged that security personnel waterboarded them and suspended them from a metal bar and beat them. Findlay alleged that he was kept in solitary confinement in Mwembeshi Correctional Facility and denied access to his prescription medication. Mwansa alleged that he suffered serious injuries, including cuts to his face and a fracture on his hand, but was denied access to medical attention. Family members told Human Rights Watch that when they found Mutyoka on August 17 at Lusaka’s Central Police Station, three days after military detained him at Mundubile’s home, he showed signs of having been physically abused. “When we saw him, his face was swollen, he was coughing blood and was limping,” a relative said. “He said they had been made to lie down in the yard of Mundubile’s home and beaten using rifle butts and whips by masked men in military unform. All he wanted was to see a doctor, but that request was denied and, to this day, he has not been seen by a doctor.” When Chewe’s family members found him at Kabwata Police Station three days after he was taken from Mundubile’s home, they said that he too showed signs of physical abuse. “He had a swollen forehead, busted lips, and complained of body pains,” a relative said. “He said he had been assaulted by the military at their headquarters before they took him to the police station.” Lawyers for Chewe, Mutyoka, and Soko at Mwembeshi Correctional Facility said that Zambia Army Special Forces personnel interrogated them and that on September 10, authorities moved the three to Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison without informing family or lawyers. On October 27, family members said medical doctors have not yet seen the three despite urgent letters written on September 9, seen by Human Rights Watch, to the commissioner of the Zambia Correctional Service and the officer-in-charge of Mwembeshi Correctional Facility. Eight election monitors for the opposition, men aged 21 to 26, said a group of armed soldiers wearing uniforms and masks jumped over the perimeter wall into a house in Lusaka’s Emmasdale township on August 15 around 8 p.m., where the monitors were meeting. They said the armed soldiers dragged them out of the house, kicked them with boots, and beat them with fists and sticks. They were forced into a military truck and taken away but could not identify where they were held. For the next three days, security forces beat them several times a day, demanding confessions that they belonged to “Brian Mundubile’s militia.” All eight were released on August 18 without charge. Human Rights Watch has also examined a petition filed on September 11 by lawyers for the 18 accused of treason that implicates the army in interrogations and abuse of detainees. In the petition, lawyers allege that special forces personnel led by Gen. Moses Shapwaya threatened and intimidated some of the detainees in prison to force them to incriminate Mundubile and Zulu. Arbitrary Arrests and Detention From court records and interviews with victims, family, and lawyers, Human Rights Watch documented 71 cases in which opposition members and supporters, as well as government critics, were arrested on charges that may be politically motivated or held in prolonged detention without charge. These include the 43 election monitors and 17 musicians and comedians who were detained after performing at an opposition rally, among others. The arrest of the 43 monitors came after the opposition leader stated that he planned to challenge the election result in court, while the government accused him of plotting an insurgency. In an electoral court challenge, the monitors would have been potential witnesses for the opposition’s case. After their 21 days in detention without charge, the court ruled that their arrest was unjustified and ordered their immediate release. Human Rights Watch interviewed a 44-year-old Lusaka mathematician who was hired to tally numbers for a potential court challenge to President Hichilema’s election. He said that on August 15 at about 9:30 p.m., about eight armed men who identified themselves as intelligence and police officers broke into his house and harassed him. They demanded access to his phone and laptop, he said, and to know who was funding the court challenge. He said they dragged him outside, put him into a vehicle, and took him to the police headquarters in Lusaka, where he was interrogated further about the election petition. The next day, he was transferred to Ridgeway Police Station, where he spent 18 days without being charged. On August 28, his lawyer filed a habeas corpus application in the Lusaka High Court, which Human Rights Watch has seen. Five days later, police charged him with a misdemeanor offense and released him the same day. Before the election, on August 5, a group of 17 people were arrested after performing at an opposition rally in Mongu, Western province. Police detained them for over two weeks on what was initially said to be a traffic offense of travelling in a vehicle without numbered plates, a lawyer familiar with the case told Human Rights Watch. The lawyer said that the group’s arrest and prolonged detention were politically motivated because of their vocal and visible mobilization for the opposition. Police later charged and prosecuted the 17 for “riotous assembly or behavior.” In a court document seen by Human Rights Watch, the state alleges that the 17 did “unlawfully assemble and begun to execute a common purpose by a breach of peace and the terror of the public.” A court released them on bail on August 30, after over three weeks in detention. Driven into Hiding Human Rights Watch interviewed seven people, including lawyers and a journalist, who said they had fled their homes because they believed they had been targeted for arrest in the days after the August 13 election. A lawyer and a journalist showed Human Rights Watch messages on their phones alerting them that they were on a “wanted list.” Some left and others were in hiding within the country. A statement by seven international lawyers’ associations said some lawyers involved in preparing or lodging election-related legal challenges had fled Zambia due to threats to their safety. A lawyer said that he went into hiding on August 15 after scores of security agents came to his home and office. The lawyer had been acting on behalf of Tonse Alliance, including working on a court petition to challenge President Hichilema’s election. “There was no reason for the security agents to chase me in that manner,” he said. “If the police wanted me for any reason, they should have alerted me, and I would have presented myself with my legal representatives.” Mulenga Kapwepwe, an opposition leader who worked closely with Mundubile and Zulu, said she went into hiding on August 15 after confidential sources alerted her that she was “on a wanted list.” “I have had to rearrange my life,” she said. “Many of my colleagues are in detention charged with treason, and I have been warned that the moment I come out of hiding, I will be targeted.” On August 17, a journalist who runs an investigative journalism website and has previously been detained for his journalism crossed the border into a neighboring country hours before security agents went to his house looking for him. “My website was following up on the raid at Mundubile’s house,” he said. “That is when I received messages on my phone saying: ‘Stop what you are doing. We are coming after you.’ I was once arrested and detained without charge for nearly two weeks. I know what these people are capable of. So, fearful for my life, I left.” While he was fleeing, the journalist said, he received a call from a family member that about five people who identified themselves as officers from Office of the President were at his house looking for him. They told his family that he was wanted for sedition. Harassment of Family Members Human Rights Watch documented two cases in which the authorities allegedly harassed and threatened the Zambia-based family members of government critics living abroad. Police allegedly detained two siblings of a well-known diaspora critic of the government and harassed their 76-year-old father, demanding that their sibling abroad, who runs a popular social media page with hundreds of thousands of followers, take down material critical of the government. One sibling was detained in a 3 a.m. raid on their home, in which armed police officers demanded access to their phones and laptop, a close source said, adding that one of the police officers “had a gun and said: ‘This is a high security operation.” The officers said the foreign-based sibling’s “political commentary was ‘a problem’ and that they needed it to stop.” The authorities allegedly demanded the removal of specific videos as a condition for their release. In one of these videos, the social media personality demanded an independent inquiry into the August 14 killing of Kafwaya. In another case, a government critic in the United States with investments in Zambia said that three men who identified themselves as intelligence officers from the Office of the President approached family members in Zambia days after the election and threatened to “squeeze” her businesses if she continued to criticize President Hichilema’s administration on social media. “They told my sister, a civil servant, that she risked losing her job if I did not tone down my criticism,” the critic said.

items.title: Petrol drops to GH¢16.38, diesel rises to GH¢18.45 as OMCs adjust pump prices
items.description: Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have begun adjusting pump prices for the first pricing window in November, with petrol prices falling and diesel prices rising. Star Oil took the lead over the weekend, reducing petrol from GH¢16.45 to GH¢16.38 per litre. It increased diesel from GH¢17.95 to GH¢18.45 per litre. Other major fuel retailers told JoyBusiness they will adjust prices later today or later this week. The changes follow projections by the Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies (COMAC) for the November 1–15, 2026 pricing window. The chamber projected a reduction of up to 3.35% in petrol prices, a 1.50% increase in diesel prices, and a 0.81% rise in liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices. Separate indicative figures from JoyBusiness put petrol at GH¢17.02 per litre and diesel at GH¢18.99. Actual pump prices will vary across marketing companies. COMAC attributed the mixed outlook to changes in international petroleum prices, a stronger cedi and government–industry intervention to cushion diesel consumers. Crude oil prices fell by 1.90% during the review period, but refined product prices moved in different directions. International petrol prices declined by 4.97%, while diesel prices rose by 3.54%. LPG prices rose the most, up 21.33%. The cedi, meanwhile, appreciated by 0.70% to GH¢11.7326 to the US dollar. This was based on average bank rates between October 12 and October 27, 2026. According to COMAC, foreign exchange interventions by the Ghana Gold Board over the past three weeks provided modest support for the currency. The chamber also cited a planned $1.5 billion injection to support the cedi ahead of the festive period. The stronger currency is expected to help moderate the impact of international price increases on consumers. For diesel, adjustments to the Energy Sector Shortfall and Debt Repayment Levy and selected statutory margins remain in place for one month to cushion the increase. “The total value of the intervention remains unchanged, maintaining the Government–industry burden-sharing arrangement introduced on 16 April 2026 to moderate increases in diesel prices at the pumps,” COMAC said.

items.title: Ethiopian PM puts ministers through military training
items.description: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country’s development. Photos he shared on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers, and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre. The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials rarely undergo military training. Participants include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa, and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last. In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia’s ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable. He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership. “Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory,” he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both. Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives. The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia. It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government’s ambitions.

items.title: China state broadcaster pulls Real Madrid match over Mbappé joke
items.description: China’s state broadcaster CCTV did not air a Real Madrid match on Sunday, despite an apology from the club’s star striker, Kylian Mbappé, for his “ill-judged” remarks about the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong. Mbappé drew huge backlash after saying the meme “that makes [him] laugh the most” was the one in which his face is superimposed on a “Chinese dictator” resembling Mao. China Media Group, CCTV’s parent organisation, said last Tuesday it would suspend broadcasts of Spanish football La Liga matches after the furore, which also led several Chinese brands to drop Mbappé. China’s foreign ministry had said it took Mbappé’s apology “seriously”. Real Madrid and La Liga have also apologised. China Media Group had earlier demanded apologies from the three parties, calling them “an absolute prerequisite” for moving past the incident. It has acknowledged the apologies but has not said how long the broadcast blackout will last. Mbappé, who reportedly made his remark about the meme on French talk show The Bridge, apologised later on Tuesday. “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,” he had said. The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his having overseen one of the bloodiest chapters in the country’s past. Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China, died in 1976. During his rule he oversaw the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society. This is not the first time Beijing has suspended sports broadcasts over political sensitivities. It pulled NBA games for a year from October 2019 after Daryl Morey, the general manager of Houston Rockets, tweeted in support of Hong Kong protesters during widespread pro-democracy protests in the city. Morey later backtracked after fierce criticism from Chinese fans, sponsors, and commercial partners. “I have had a lot of opportunity since that tweet to hear and consider other perspectives,” Morey later wrote. “I have always appreciated the significant support our Chinese fans and sponsors…I would hope that those who are upset will know that offending or misunderstanding them was not my intention.” Real Madrid beat Racing Santander 3-0 on Sunday, with goals from Mbappé, Jude Bellingham, and Yan Diomande.

items.title: Canada, US working towards a new trade deal after Carney, Trump call
items.description: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday that he had a "good conversation" with US President Donald Trump on the future of Canada-US trade. Carney said on social media that the discussion built on "recent constructive discussions on the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal" that would create jobs, improve affordability, and fully respect Canada's languages, culture and sovereignty. "Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome," Carney ⁠wrote on X. US President Donald Trump said ⁠on Sunday that his administration has the "concept" of a new trade deal with Canada after speaking with Carney. "I ‌spoke to him again yesterday, and we have the concept of ‌a deal that's going to be great for our farmers, ‌great for our country, and we'll be fine for that," Trump told reporters in Dubuque, Iowa. Carney's latest statement followed comments he made to US media outlet Politico just two days earlier, when he insisted he was in no hurry to strike a trade truce with Trump and would wait out his presidency until 2029, rather than sign an unfavorable deal. "What is happening is that every month that goes by, Canada grows stronger," Carney said, according to Politico. "Our options increase." Canada ‌and the United States have slapped billions of dollars in tariffs on each other in recent months. The imposition of tariffs on Canada has emerged as an issue in some northern US border states like Michigan and Maine before US midterm elections on Tuesday. Trump said last week that a trade deal with Canada ‌was coming soon, but Ottawa had previously reported limited progress in trade talks, despite efforts to ease tariffs on steel and autos. Trump said on Sunday that the ​scope of an agreement would include the Keystone XL pipeline project that he supports, though it was not immediately clear how the project would be revived. A spokesperson for Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for ⁠trade with the US, had no further comment on Sunday ⁠evening beyond Carney's remarks. Trump said in August that the pipeline "may be awoken from the grave." The ​proposed pipeline would have carried 830,000 barrels per ​day of oil from the oil sands of northern Alberta to the major US ‌storage hub at Cushing, Oklahoma, and then on to Gulf Coast refineries. Canada, the world's fourth-largest oil exporter, sends more than ‌90% of its crude oil production to the ⁠US. (With input from agencies)

items.title: Kabul warned of ‘unbearable punishment’ as clashes persist along border
items.description: • Torkham stays shut for five hours following firefight over disputed check post • Military spox says Afghan Taliban ‘won’t be able to bear cost’ of harbouring terrorists • Names India as ‘prime contractor’ behind terrorism in Pakistan • Rubio says US shares Pakistan’s concerns over attacks from Afghan soil, open to role in easing tensions KHYBER/LOWER SOUTH WAZIRISTAN: Pakistani and Afghan border forces exchanged fire at several points along their border on Sunday, as the military warned that the Afghan Taliban would not be able to withstand the “punishment” Islamabad could inflict if Kabul failed to rein in terrorists. The fresh clashes temporarily shut down the busy Torkham border crossing over a disputed check post and killed one civilian in mortar shelling near the Angoor Adda crossing. The situation unfolded as Washington validated Pakistan’s concerns regarding cross-border terrorist attacks originating from Afghanistan and signalled openness to playing a productive role in easing tensions. The situation at the Torkham cro­ssing stabilised after a nearly five-hour closure caused by an hou­rlong exchange of light-arms fire. It reopened only after border officials from both countries agreed through intermediaries to halt all construction near the border. However, tensions remained high in the Angoor Adda area of Lower South Waziristan. According to the deputy commissioner of Lower South Wazir­istan, Taliban fighters continued to target Pakistani border checkpoints with unprovoked firing. Pakistani security forces responded immediately and effectively, targeting “multiple Afghan border posts, mortar positions, and defensive checkpoints”, the official wrote on X, adding that no reports of any casualties have emerged from the border areas on the Pakistani side. Border clashes According to locals, gunfire erupted at Torkham on Sunday when Afghan authorities once again started construction on a disputed check post. Authorities at Torkham said the Afghan side began work on the controversial Zangali check post, situated within a 100-metre radius of the Afghan side of the border, despite Pakistan’s strong objections. The firing continued for nearly an hour with no casualties on the Pakistani side. The two nations had previously agreed to refrain from building security structures within a 100-metre radius of the border. The intense firing caused the immediate closure of the border and panic among returning Afghans and local residents. During the standoff, resident Siraj Khan told Dawn that he saw about 20 vehicles carrying unregistered Afghan families hastily returning from the border at Zero Point amid the crossfire. The repatriation of unregistered Afghans was suspended, and government offices were closed. Meanwhile, tensions escalated in the Angoor Adda area after two mortar shells were reportedly fired from the Afghan side. Military’s warning The flare-ups underscored a stark warning delivered by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) chief, Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry. In an interview with a news agency earlier this week, portions of which were broadcast by state media on Sunday, the military’s spokesperson said Pakistan has the operational readiness and a clear strategy to impose a heavy cost on the interim Afghan leadership if terrorism continues originating from Afghan soil. “Whatever they want to send, they can, they may try. We have the capability to take them out,” Lt Gen Chaudhry said. “They don’t have, I think, the capability to then absorb the punishment that we can [inflict].” He noted that Pakistan has no desire to interfere in Afghanistan’s internal governance. “We only ask that you don’t support terrorism inside Pakistan. Stop harbouring the terrorist leaders,” he added. The ISPR chief asserted that while foreign military forces have physically withdrawn from Afghanistan, the Afghan Taliban front continues to operate as a proxy for multiple external parties, singling out India as the primary sponsor of anti-Pakistan terrorism. “In the case of Pakistan, the prime contractor is India, and the proxies are TTP and the BLA,” he said, describing New Delhi as “the biggest terror sponsor here” and stating that “as far as terrorism in Pakistan is concerned, they [the Afghan Taliban] are a proxy of the Indians”. Addressing whether Pakistan fears a cross-border drone dynamic similar to Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, Lt Gen Chaudhry noted Afghanistan has no domestic drone industry and relies entirely on external sponsors. “The capability of Afghans, whatever they have, firstly it’s not their own. There’s no drone industry, there is no technology of that sort in Afghanistan. So it’s been provided by the sponsors, the terror sponsors, because the biggest terror sponsor here is India,” he said. The ISPR chief emphasised that the Pakistan Army is systematically adapting to the changing character of modern warfare across contact and non-contact domains, cyber operations, drones and long-range munitions. US shares Pakistan’s concerns The security concerns were echoed in Washington’s diplomatic messaging, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio affirmed that the US shares Pakistan’s concerns regarding cross-border terrorist attacks originating from Afghanistan and signalled openness to playing a productive role in easing tensions. “We don’t want Pakistan to be targeted for terrorism,” he told reporters at the G20 foreign ministers meeting in Atlanta, Georgia. “Pakistan is concerned about terrorist attacks that are being sponsored from the territory of Afghanistan. They think that the Taliban has not done enough to constrain those attacks,” Mr Rubio said, noting that Pakistan had taken action in response to the threat. He added that Washington did not have close relations with the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan and the US opposed terrorism regardless of where it originated or whom it targeted. “We’ve heard the concerns that Pakistan has raised, and we’ve seen some of those attacks that they point to,” Rubio said. “We’re against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets.” With input from APP Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

items.title: US-backed consortium proposes $4.4bn LNG project
items.description: • Proposal envisages four tanks holding 560,000 cubic metres at Port Qasim in first phase of the $4.4bn plan that also includes a 1,100km upcountry gas pipeline • Project would charge $4.93 per mmBtu for terminal and storage, $1.91 for transmission over first decade ISLAMABAD: A private consortium of US companies, backed by the Trump administration, is pushing for an investment of up to $4.4 billion in an integrated liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Pakistan, covering imports, storage, re-gasification, gas transmission and sales to large consumers on a ‘merchant basis’. The development comes after Energas, an earlier frontrunner consisting of the Lucky Group and QatarEnergy, abandoned a similar project citing fundamental changes in Pakistan’s energy policy and requirements, as well as longstanding unresolved policy and fiscal issues. The US consortium comprises Global Vision Energy Partners (GVEP) and Khanjee Holdings, both related firms, along with strategic co-investors from other countries and General Mediterranean Holding, a Luxem­bo­urg-based US financial conglomerate. The sponsors have reportedly sec­ured consent from the Port Qasim Aut­hority for the proposed project site. An application has also been filed with the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) for a provisional licence. A special purpose vehicle (SPV), a separate legal entity established to hold specific assets and liabilities and isolate financial risks, has been incorporated. Government facilitation has also been conveyed through the Mini­stry of Maritime Affairs and the Mini­stry of Energy’s Petroleum Divi­sion, according to documents seen by Dawn. The project has been approved for consideration under the US Trade and Development Agency’s (USTDA) project preparation programme. It may also receive partial financing from the US Development Finance Corporation, backed by export credit guarantees from the US Export-Import Bank for technology, equipment and services. Pakistan currently has no LNG storage facilities, leaving its domestic re-gasified LNG supplies entirely dependent on import supply chains and international energy prices. The sponsors plan to develop the project in two phases. The first phase will comprise an LNG terminal and storage facility with four tanks and an estimated annual throughput of 35 billion cubic feet (BCF), at a cost of $1.7bn. The second phase will involve the construction of a 1,100km, 42-48-inch pipeline to transport gas upcountry, with a capacity of around 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (BCFD). This will take the total project cost to $4.4bn. The government had previously pursued a similar North-South gas pipeline project with Russia. The proposed venture is being structured as a merchant infrastructure platform to meet domestic regasification requirements while establishing a physical LNG storage and trading hub in South Asia for US and Middle Eastern suppliers. The consortium is engaging local inve­stors for up to 10 per cent equity participation, with indicative investments starting at $50 million per investor. The sponsors also expect to attract strategic co-investors, including global energy and infrastructure funds and institutional investors such as Grey Rock Investment Partners, Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co, Blackstone Inc., Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and the Kuwait Investment Authority. Their participation remains subject to due diligence, investment approvals and definitive agreements. No binding equity commitments have been confirmed so far. The SPV will develop, own and operate the project as a regional LNG storage, regasification and trading hub, serving Pakistan’s domestic gas market alongside US and Middle Eastern LNG suppliers. The model will not depend on a single government-backed offtake arrangement. Re-gasification tariffs for the domestic market will be submitted to Ogra for approval, while other commercial services, including storage, tolling and transshipment, will be priced on market-based terms. The US sponsors consider Port Qasim strategically important because of its existing port infrastructure and marine access for LNG carriers. Its location outside the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most significant energy shipping chokepoints, is another key consideration. Under the proposed financing structure, the project will have a 70:30 debt-to-equity ratio. GVEP will hold a 26pc stake, followed by General Mediterranean Holding with 24pc, and Khanjee Holdings and strategic co-investors with 20pc each. Local investors will hold the remaining 10pc in the first phase, which is estimated to cost $1.32bn (70pc of the $1.7bn cost). The final project cost will be determined after the execution of engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts and other construction and supply agreements. The commercial model is expected to combine long-term tolling and storage agreements, transshipment arrangements and take-or-pay commitments where appropriate, with the remaining capacity reserved for merchant activities. The proposed tolling tariff for the terminal and storage facility is $4.93 per million British thermal units (mmBtu), while the separate transmission tariff is estimated at $1.91 per mmBtu for the first 10 years. These rates are projected to decline to $2.20 and $0.92 per mmBtu, respectively, thereafter. The LNG terminal and storage facility will have four tanks, each with a capacity of 140,000 cubic metres, providing total static storage capacity of 560,000 cubic metres. Based on three inventory turnover cycles annually, the facility is expected to handle approximately 35.6BCF of LNG a year, with storage capacity of around 11.9BCF per cycle. Published in Dawn, November 2nd, 2026

items.title: Yerevan Pathway sets course for biodiversity action
items.description: The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) concluded in Yerevan, Armenia, on Saturday after negotiators secured agreement on the conference's main decisions, including the Yerevan Pathway aimed at accelerating global biodiversity action. This encouraging outcome came at a critical time for global biodiversity protection. Halfway between the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and its 2030 deadline, countries face a widening gap between their commitments to protect nature and the action to fulfill them. Whether the Yerevan Pathway can help close that gap will depend on financing, national policies and sustained international cooperation. A pathway to accelerate action The conference's main task was to conduct the first global review of collective progress in implementing the GBF, which sets out 23 targets for 2030. The assessment presented governments with a clear warning: Without a rapid acceleration of implementation, the framework's 2030 targets and mission would not be achieved, putting its longer-term goals for 2050 at risk. The Yerevan Pathway is part of the response to that assessment. Rather than setting new targets, it focuses on how countries can step up efforts to meet those already agreed upon. Embedded in the global review decision, the pathway identifies several priorities for the period through 2030: accelerating implementation, broadening the coverage of national targets, strengthening financial and other support, engaging governments and societies more widely, and improving monitoring and knowledge. Alongside the negotiations, nearly $2 billion in new biodiversity funding was announced, according to the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). This included $560 million under the ninth replenishment of the Global Environment Facility and its Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, $500 million through the Species Recovery Alliance and more than $330 million through the Value Nature Fund. Finance divide tests delivery Finance remains one of the main obstacles to implementation, both in terms of how much funding is available and how the responsibility for providing it is shared. The global report found that developed countries had failed to meet their commitment to provide at least $20 billion annually in biodiversity finance to developing countries by 2025. This shortfall was a major point of contention in negotiations over funding for the next stage of implementation. Some developed countries called for broadening the contributor base, bringing into focus a longstanding dispute over the relationship between countries' financial capacity and their obligations under the CBD. The new funding announcements offered some encouragement, but the broader challenge of securing predictable support on the scale needed remains. For developing countries, efforts to strengthen conservation, restore ecosystems and monitor progress continue to depend heavily on access to finance and technical assistance. China's role in advancing implementation Turning commitments into concrete results was also a key theme in discussions of China's contribution, including its support for the global review, sharing experience in domestic conservation and financing for biodiversity projects in developing countries. The global review decision specifically thanked China for hosting the Kunming dialogue to support preparations for the review. It also acknowledged financial support provided through the China Trust Fund via the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP). During the conference, COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan said China had made important contributions to advancing the talks, from preparatory work to the formal negotiations. Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the secretariat of the CBD, said the progress reflected in China's seventh national report was encouraging and highlighted its ecological conservation red lines as an example of how biodiversity protection could be incorporated into national planning and development. Inger Andersen, executive director of the UNEP, recognized China's continued leadership through the establishment of the Kunming Biodiversity Fund following its COP15 presidency. She emphasized the importance of helping developing countries access the financing needed to implement the agreement. The Yerevan conference preserved a common direction at a difficult moment for biodiversity protection. The next four years will determine whether governments can turn their commitments into measurable progress before the 2030 deadline. As Schomaker put it: "Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home."
